These processes are essential for human reproduction and the continuation of life.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

TargetRLF1: While some people with Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes will never have any symptoms, other people can develop symptoms within a few weeks of being infected. Common oral herpes symptoms include blisters (cold sores) or open sores (ulcers) in or around the mouth or lips. Most people notice a group or cluster of blisters or ulcers (lesions). In case of Neonatal Herpes, signs that your baby may have herpes are:irritability, blisters anywhere on her body, trouble breathing, grunting, blue appearance (cyanosis), rapid breathing, short periods of no breathing, jaundice, bleeding easily. People can have repeated outbreaks over time (‘recurrences’). These are usually shorter and less severe than the first outbreak. Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

TargetRLF1: The only way to completely avoid STIs is to not have vaginal, anal, or oral sex. If you are sexually active, you can do the following things to lower your chances of getting Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes:•        Being in a long-term mutually monogamous relationship with a partner who does not have herpes.•        Using condoms the right way every time you have sex.Be aware that not all herpes sores occur in areas that a condom can cover. Also, the skin can release the virus (shed) from areas that do not have a visible herpes sore. For these reasons, condoms may not fully protect you from getting herpes. If your sex partner(s) has/have genital herpes, you can lower your risk of getting it if:•        Your partner takes an anti-herpes medicine every day. This is something your partner should discuss with his or her healthcare provider.•        You avoid having vaginal, anal, or oral sex when your partner has herpes symptoms (i.e., during an "outbreak").If you are pregnant and have genital herpes, prenatal care visits are very important. Some research suggest that a genital herpes infection may lead to miscarriage or make it more likely to deliver your baby too early. You can pass herpes to your unborn child before birth, but it more commonly passes during delivery. This can lead to a deadly infection in your baby (called neonatal herpes). It is important that you avoid getting genital herpes during pregnancy. Tell your healthcare provider if you have ever had a genital herpes diagnosis or symptoms. Also tell them about any possible exposure to genital herpes. If you have genital herpes, you may need to take anti-herpes medicine towards the end of your pregnancy. This medicine may reduce your risk of having signs or symptoms of genital herpes when you deliver. At the time of delivery, your healthcare provider should carefully examine you for herpes sores. If you have signs or symptoms of genital herpes at delivery, a 'C-section' is likely to occur.

TargetRLF1: Uncomplicated Chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection can be easily cured with antibiotics and is usually resolved within days or weeks. It is important that you take all of the medicine your healthcare provider gives you because untreated or improperly treated Chlamydia can lead to serious complications. Do not share medicine for chlamydia with anyone. Recommended drugs include Doxycylcine, Azithromycin, Levofloxacin and Amoxicillin. When taken properly, drugs will stop the infection and could decrease your chances of having problems later. Although medicine will stop the infection, it will not undo any permanent damage caused by the disease. You should notify your sexual partner(s) to get tested and treated, if necessary. Repeat infection with chlamydia is common. You should receive testing again about three months after your treatment, even if your sex partner(s) receives treatment. If the mother had a documented chlamydial infection during pregnancy that was untreated, presumptively treat the infant, even without confirmation of infection.

The early stage of syphilis is treated with a benzathine penicillin (BPG) injection. BPG is the first line treatment for syphilis and the only WHO-recommended treatment for pregnant women with syphilis. As second line treatment, doctors may also use doxycycline, ceftriaxone or azithromycin, which are antibiotic medicines is also used to treat later stages of syphilis, but more doses are required. Doses are usually given once per week for three weeks, including when it is not possible to identify the stage of infection. Your partner should also get treatment. Do not have sex (vaginal, anal or oral) until you and your partner have finished treatment and tests have shown treatment has worked. BPG can prevent syphilis from being passed from a mother to baby. Babies born with syphilis (congenital syphilis), or babies whose mother had untreated syphilis, need to be treated right away to avoid serious health problems. Aqueous benzyl penicillin or procaine penicillin is recommended in infants with confirmed congenital syphilis or infants who are clinically healthy but whose mothers had untreated syphilis, inadequately treated syphilis (including treatment within 30 days of delivery), or syphilis treated with non-penicillin regimens. Unfortunately, while Syphilis can be cured, there is no way to repair organs damaged by syphilis.

TargetRLF1: While some people with Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes will never have any symptoms, other people can develop symptoms within a few weeks of being infected. Common oral herpes symptoms include blisters (cold sores) or open sores (ulcers) in or around the mouth or lips. Most people notice a group or cluster of blisters or ulcers (lesions). These lesions burn and can be painful. They can appear on the buttocks, anus or thighs, on the vulva or vagina in women, and on the penis or scrotum in men. Often, before the lesions appear, patients describe a prodrome, characterized by a tingling or burning sensation in the area where the lesions will develop that can be noticed during urination, along with itching or discomfort in the genital area. You can also have the following symptoms, Blisters on the mouth or lips, Fever, headache or pain in the joints, Trouble urinating. In case of Neonatal Herpes, signs that your baby may have herpes are:irritability, blisters anywhere on her body, trouble breathing, grunting, blue appearance (cyanosis), rapid breathing, short periods of no breathing, jaundice, bleeding easily. People can have repeated outbreaks over time (‘recurrences’). These are usually shorter and less severe than the first outbreak. Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

TargetRLF1: Chlamydia infections also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary Infections spread through sexual contact, when vaginal fluid or semen containing the bacteria that causes chlamydia travels from one person to another. Oral sex; bacteria pass from one person’s mouth to their partner’s penis, vagina or anus, or vice versa. For example, this can happen if you touch the genitals of an infected person and then rub your eyes without washing your hands first. A pregnant person with chlamydia can give the infection to their baby during childbirth and that can cause a type of eye infection in the baby which can damage their sight.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI) so as to get treatment. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing. Results are usually ready in a day. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

If you are sexually active, you can do the following things to lower your chances of getting Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes:•        Being in a long-term mutually monogamous relationship with a partner who does not have herpes.•        Using condoms the right way every time you have sex.Be aware that not all herpes sores occur in areas that a condom can cover. This medicine may reduce your risk of having signs or symptoms of genital herpes when you deliver. At the time of delivery, your healthcare provider should carefully examine you for herpes sores. If you have signs or symptoms of genital herpes at delivery, a 'C-section' is likely to occur.

This medicine may reduce your chances of having signs or symptoms of herpes of the private parts when you deliver. TargetRLF1: While some people with Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes will never have any symptoms, other people can develop symptoms within a few weeks of being infected. Common oral herpes symptoms include blisters (cold sores) or open sores (ulcers) in or around the mouth or lips. Most people notice a group or cluster of blisters or ulcers (lesions). These lesions burn and can be painful. They can appear on the buttocks, anus or thighs, on the vulva or vagina in women, and on the penis or scrotum in men. Often, before the lesions appear, patients describe a prodrome, characterized by a tingling or burning sensation in the area where the lesions will develop that can be noticed during urination, along with itching or discomfort in the genital area. You can also have the following symptoms, Blisters on the mouth or lips, Fever, headache or pain in the joints, Trouble urinating. In case of Neonatal Herpes, signs that your baby may have herpes are:irritability, blisters anywhere on her body, trouble breathing, grunting, blue appearance (cyanosis), rapid breathing, short periods of no breathing, jaundice, bleeding easily. People can have repeated outbreaks over time (‘recurrences’). These are usually shorter and less severe than the first outbreak. Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

If symptoms occur, they may not appear until several weeks after having sex with a partner who has chlamydia. Even when chlamydia has no symptoms, it can damage a woman's reproductive system. Women with symptoms of Genital infection may notice: An abnormal vaginal discharge, A burning sensation when peeing. Men with symptoms of Genital infection may notice: A discharge from their penis, A burning sensation when peeing, Pain and swelling in one or both testicles (although this is less common). Symptoms from rectal infections. Men and women can also get chlamydia in their rectum. This happens either by having receptive anal sex, or by spread from another infected site (such as the vagina). If a patient has Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV), initial symptoms may include genital ulcers, followed by painful swelling of lymph nodes in the groin. If untreated, it can lead to severe complications such as rectal strictures.  Throat infections can cause symptoms such as swelling in the back of the throat and mild sore throat, but symptoms are rare.

TargetRLF1: Gonorrhea can be traced back to the earliest records of the human race. The Romans, Jews and Arabs all have documents referring to gonorrhea and each society had their own description of symptoms and treatment. The origins of Gonorrhea can be traced back to the Old Testament in the books of Leviticus and Genesis where it is described as a contagious, continuous passing out of semen and painful erection. In those days, men were considered victims and women as the source of the disease. The organism that causes the disease was first discovered in 1879 in Albert Neisser, hence the organisma being called Neisseria Gonorrhoea. The word Gonorrhea itself derives from the Greek, meaning "the flow of seed" (gono: seed, rhea: flow).

Congenital syphilis can only be prevented by diagnosing and treating the mother.

TargetRLF1: Human immunodeficiency virus is an infection that originated in animals and passed into human hosts. It is closely related to the simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) found in chimpanzees in central Africa. To date, the earliest known case of HIV-1 infection in human blood is from a sample taken in 1959 from a man who died in Kinshasa in what was then the Belgian Congo. SIV probably entered the human population as a result of hunting chimpanzees. It is plausible that transmission could have occurred through a hunter being wounded and blood from a chimpanzee entering his bloodstream.  The origin of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) has been a subject of scientific research and debate since the virus was identified in the 1980s.

PrEP kwa kawaida huchukuliwa kwa njia ya dawa ya kumeza ya kila siku, kwa kawaida mchanganyiko wa tenofovir na emtricitabine (jina la chapa Truvada) au tenofovir alafenamide na emtricitabine (jina la chapa Descovy). Hivi ndivyo PrEP inavyosaidia: Kuzuia Maambukizi ya virusi vya ukimwi, Kuzuia Kujirudia kwa virusi vya ukimwi, Kudumisha Kiwango cha Kinga, Kupunguza Hatari ya Maambukizi, Kupatikana na Rafiki kwa Mtumiaji, na Kuunga mkono Mienendo ya Ngono Salama. Ni muhimu kutambua kwamba PrEP ni bora zaidi inapochukuliwa mara kwa mara na kama ilivyoagizwa. Kukosekana kwa dozi au matumizi yasiyo ya kawaida kunaweza kupunguza ufanisi wake. Zaidi ya hayo, PrEP hailinde dhidi ya magonjwa mengine ya zinaa (STIs), hivyo watu binafsi wanapaswa bado kutumia kondomu na kushiriki katika mazoea mengine ya ngono salama ili kuzuia magonjwa ya zinaa. PrEP inapendekezwa kwa watu walio katika hatari kubwa ya kuambukizwa virusi vya ukimwi, ikiwa ni pamoja na wale walio katika uhusiano usio na usawa (ambapo mpenzi mmoja ana virusi vya ukimwi na mwingine hana virusi vya ukimwi), wanaume wanaofanya ngono na wanaume, watu wanaojidunga madawa ya kulevya, na watu binafsi. na wapenzi wengi wa ngono. Ni muhimu kushauriana na mhudumu wa afya ili kubaini kama PrEP inafaa na kupokea ufuatiliaji na upimaji wa mara kwa mara unapotumia dawa. PrEP inaweza kuwa nyenzo muhimu katika kuzuia virusi vya ukimwi inapotumiwa kwa usahihi pamoja na hatua nyingine za kuzuia.
